catalog_quote: p. 27: "Perlu diingatkan bahwa tekanan kata dalam bahasa Mandar pada umumnya jatuh pada suku kedua dari belakang, baik yang bersuku dua, bersuku tiga maupun yang bersuku empat. Untuk beberapa kata yang bersuku, tiga tekanannya jatuh pada suku pertama dari belakang, seperti: /arabaq/ 'Rabu' /arrua/ 'delapan' /amessa/ 'sembilan' Kata-kata yang bersuku satu vokalnya menjadi agak panjang karena pengaruh tekanan ini. Hal ini ada hubungannya dengan sintagmatis serta fungsi kata itu dalam satu konteks kalimat." [Translation: It should be remembered that word stress in Mandar generally falls on the second syllable from the end, whether the word has two, three or four syllables. For a few three-syllable words the stress falls on the first syllable from the end, e.g. /arabaq/ 'Wednesday', /arrua/ 'eight', /amessa/ 'nine'. Words of one syllable have their vowel become somewhat long under the influence of this stress. This is connected with syntagmatics and the function of the word in a sentence context.] Brodkin 2025 NLLT sec. 2.2.1: "This stress surfaces once per word and falls on the penultimate syllable (Pelenkahu et al. 1983), and its most salient phonetic correlate is a low tone (co-occurring with increases in amplitude and length)." ex. (18) óro / oróaN / oroánna 'to sit, a seat, her seat'.

Untuk beberapa kata yang bersuku tiga tekanannya jatuh pada suku pertama dari belakang, seperti: /arabaq/ 'Rabu', /arrua/ 'delapan', /amessa/ 'sembilan'. Kata-kata yang bersuku satu vokalnya menjadi agak panjang karena pengaruh tekanan ini. Hal ini ada hubungannya dengan sintagmatis serta fungsi kata itu dalam satu konteks kalimat.
new_statements.translation: It should be remembered that word stress in Mandar generally falls on the second syllable from the end, whether the word has two, three or four syllables. For a few three-syllable words the stress falls on the first syllable from the end [i.e. the final syllable], e.g. /arabaq/ 'Wednesday', /arrua/ 'eight', /amessa/ 'nine'. In monosyllabic words the vowel becomes somewhat long under the influence of this stress. This is connected with syntagmatics and the function of the word in a sentence context.

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (printed page 27 of Pelenkahu, Muthalib & Sangi 1983, Struktur Bahasa Mandar; title page scan-0004 confirms authors, Pusat Pembinaan dan Pengembangan Bahasa, Jakarta 1983). The quoted paragraph is there at the top of p.27 exactly as reported; the only differences are typographic: the print has a smudged 'diingatkan' and a misplaced comma ('Untuk beberapa kata yang bersuku, tiga tekanannya jatuh pada suku pertama dari belakang'), which the compilers silently normalised to 'bersuku tiga tekanannya'. The three final-stress examples /arabaq/ 'Rabu', /arrua/ 'delapan', /amessa/ 'sembilan' and the sentences on monosyllabic lengthening and syntagmatic context follow verbatim. I also viewed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable regardless of word length; word-level suffixes (e.g. -na, -aN, -i) count and pull stress rightward, whereas enclitics (e.g. absolutive =i) do not (Brodkin 2021, 2025: bóyang, boyánna, bóyang=i; óro, oróaN, oroánna). Modern fieldwork (Brodkin 2025 NLLT sec. 2.2.1) confirms: one stress per lexical word on the penult, main correlate a low tone with added amplitude and length; function heads (P, Dem, C) unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Pelenkahu et al. give a notation for primary/second/third/weak stress in intonation transcriptions (p.22) but state no word-level secondary-stress rule; Brodkin 2025 (fn.5) assumes regular secondary stress is absent in Mandar, as in Makassarese and Konjo.
new_statements.exceptions: A few trisyllabic words with final stress (arabaq 'Wednesday', arrua 'eight', amessa 'nine') per Pelenkahu et al. 1983:27; Brodkin (LI, sec. 6.1) describes a small lexical class (e.g. magarriŋ 'have a fever') that is penultimate phrase-medially but final at the right edge of the intonational phrase, and contrastively focused roots in that position also take final stress (cówa vs cowà); stress/pitch minimal pairs from suffix vs enclitic -i (báse=i 'already wet' vs baséi 'wash', mála=i vs malái) p.22.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word including suffixes but excluding enclitics (Brodkin: stress marks the right edge of the prosodic word); Pelenkahu et al. describe 'dialek-dialek Mandar' with Balanipa as the reference dialect; Brodkin's data are from the standard (Balanipa/Tinambung-area) variety. Phrase-final position can shift stress to the final syllable for certain items/foci.
new_statements.identity_note: Pelenkahu et al. 1983 describe 'dialek-dialek Mandar' with Balanipa (Polewali-Mamasa) as the reference dialect and note intonational differences among dialects (Balanipa, Majene/Banggae, Pamboang, Sendana, Awo Sumakuyu); Brodkin's fieldwork is on the standard Balanipa-area variety. All fall under mand1442; no separate glottocode needed.

sources.citation: Brodkin, Dan. 2025. The prosody of the extended VP. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory (online first; no volume/issue/pages in the PDF header). doi:10.1007/s11049-024-09634-4
sources.quote: At the metrical level in Mandar, a single instance of stress falls on every constituent that corresponds to a head at the base of an extended projection (Grimshaw 1991): N0, V0, ADJ0, and ADV0 (including many adverbs that surface in second-position). It is absent from heads that sit higher on the functional spine, such as P0, DEM0, and C0. This stress surfaces once per word and falls on the penultimate syllable (Pelenkahu et al. 1983), and its most salient phonetic correlate is a low tone (co-occurring with increases in amplitude and length).

sources.note: Sec. 6.1, ms pp.43-44: 'Mandar is a language that shows regular penultimate stress at the level of the word, and within the native vocabulary, there are few lexical exceptions to this rule (Pelenkahu et al., 1983)'; a small class of words (e.g. magarriŋ) shifts to final stress at the right edge of the intonational phrase, and contrastively focused roots there also take final stress (cówa vs cowà).

sources.note: The paper argues that Mandar shifts DP-internal locative adverbs rightward by a phonological, not syntactic, movement, and its sec. 6.1 states regular penultimate word stress with a small lexical class and contrastively focused roots taking final stress at the right edge of the intonational phrase. The data are elicited judgments from native speakers (no acoustic measurement), and the catalog entry already cites this same paper's author manuscript (sec. 6.1) as corroboration of penultimate stress.
